# The Physics Behind Towing Automatic RWD Vehicles in Neutral

Towing an automatic rear-wheel-drive (RWD) vehicle with the engine running and the transmission in neutral is a common request, often driven by the desire to save fuel or avoid idling emissions during short-distance moves. While it might seem intuitive that disengaging the gearbox via the shifter puts all moving parts to rest, the mechanical reality of an automatic transmission creates significant friction points even when the car appears stationary under its own power.

When you shift an automatic into neutral while driving on a flat surface with no load, the engine's torque converter locks up or slips minimally, and the output shaft spins freely without resistance from the wheels. However, towing introduces a variable that neutral cannot mitigate: the rear wheels are now being forced to spin by an external force rather than the engine. In a standard automatic transmission, the driveshaft connects directly to the rear differential. If you tow this vehicle in neutral, the spinning rear wheels will drive the differential, which spins the driveshaft backward into the transmission case.

This reverse rotation is where the damage occurs. Most modern automatic transmissions rely on hydraulic pressure from the engine's oil pump to lubricate internal components and actuate clutches. When the vehicle is being towed in neutral with the engine off—or even running if the torque converter doesn't engage enough to overcome the drag—the primary oil pump may not generate sufficient flow. Even if the engine is idling, the hydraulic pressure might be inconsistent compared to driving conditions. As the driveshaft spins backward, critical bearings and clutch packs experience metal-on-metal contact without adequate lubrication, leading to rapid overheating and catastrophic failure.

### The Role of the Torque Converter

There is a nuanced scenario where this practice becomes less risky: towing with the engine running. When the engine is idling, the torque converter attempts to convert rotational energy from the crankshaft into hydraulic fluid movement. In many designs, the stator in the torque converter will lock up at low RPMs if the vehicle isn't moving forward under load, effectively creating a one-way clutch mechanism that prevents reverse rotation of the turbine (connected to the transmission input).

However, this protection is not universal across all manufacturers or transmission architectures. Some torque converters allow free-wheeling in both directions during specific idle states, or the lock-up clutch may disengage entirely when the vehicle is stationary but being pulled. Relying on a proprietary mechanical behavior that varies by model year and manufacturer is a dangerous trade-off. A short distance of 50 meters might not generate enough heat to kill the transmission immediately, but it does introduce an unverified risk factor into your maintenance plan.

### Safer Alternatives for Movement

If you must move the vehicle without driving it yourself, the safest approach remains flat-towing with the engine off and the parking brake disengaged, provided the manufacturer explicitly states this is allowed. Many modern vehicles require a specific "tow mode" to be engaged via an ignition switch position or a diagnostic tool to isolate the transmission from reverse rotation forces.

For short distances where engine noise is a concern, consider using dollies for the rear wheels. This method physically lifts the driven axles off the ground, eliminating the need for the transmission to handle any rotational force. It adds complexity to the setup but guarantees zero stress on the internal components of the automatic gearbox regardless of whether the engine runs or not.

### Verdict on Short-Distance Towing

While the idea of a quick, neutral-tow with an idling engine sounds convenient, it relies on assumptions about torque converter behavior that cannot be guaranteed for every vehicle. The risk of stripping bearings and destroying clutch packs outweighs the minor benefit of avoiding idle emissions or fuel consumption during a short move. Unless you have confirmed documentation from the manufacturer stating your specific RWD model allows this operation without damage, the prudent engineering decision is to avoid it entirely.
